# Mahādhammapālajātaka (Ja 447)

**ID:** Ja 447
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahādhammapālajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Dhammapāla the Great
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja447
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul9.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahādhammapālajātaka* (Ja 447) is a canonical Pali birth-story opening with the verse *Kiṃ te vatan ti* [Fausböll 1887; SuttaCentral]. According to its frame narrative, the Buddha delivered the discourse during his first return to Kapilavatthu while residing at his father's Banyan Grove (*Nigrodhārāma*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887; Than Hsiang 2018]. King Suddhodana recounted how, during the Bodhisatta's period of austere striving (*dukkaracārikā*), a deity falsely announced that his son had died; the king had firmly refused to believe the deity because his son could not die before attaining awakening [Fausböll 1877; Gaffney 2003]. The Buddha explained that in a former birth as well, the father had refused to believe a report of his son's death even when shown bones [Burlingame 1921; Gaffney 2003]. At the end of the exposition, King Suddhodana attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1887; Gaffney 2003], while Pali traditions also associate this preaching with Mahāprajāpatī's attainment of stream-entry [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha reveals that the teacher of that past life was Sāriputta, the parents were the royal couple, and Prince Dhammapāla was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1887].

A full parallel is preserved in the Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (Mvu 42, *The Story of Dharmapāla*) [Appleton 2013; SuttaCentral], an alignment substantiated by DharmaNexus with 35 cross-language matches [DharmaNexus]. The Tibetan *Nidānakathā* refers to the text as *Chos skyon ba chen po'i skyes rabs* [Gaffney 2003], and DharmaNexus further detects alignments with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Canonical passage-level parallels occur in the *Dhammikattheragāthā* (Thag 4.10) and the *Ayogharajātaka* (Ja 510), and the story is cited in the *Nettippakaraṇa* and *Peṭakopadesa* [SuttaCentral]. Within Pali commentarial literature, DharmaNexus notes 171 matching segments across 15 texts, including the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Suttantanīti*, and *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. In Southeast Asian tradition, the story was incorporated into Siamese works such as the *Bimbābilāpasutta* and the *Paṭhamasambodhikathā* [Skilling 2002], and is attested in temple ink glosses at Pagan [Win Than Tun 2002].
